episodes.168150: A strong synoptic cyclone swinging into the Northern Plains set the stage for a late Spring severe weather outbreak on May 30th. Discrete and semi-discrete supercells developed during the afternoon ahead of an arcing cold front and a nearby surface low. These storms quickly traveled northeast while gradually growing upscale into bowing line segments as storms merged together and new cells formed. During this time, hail and tornadoes occurred; the strongest being an EF2 through Forada, MN. The bowing line segments became dominant and a wind event unfolded.||Strong and broad synoptic lift, little capping, and questionable mid-level shear likely allowed for upscale growth. This caused storm interactions and competing updrafts which may have limited mesocyclone longevity and strength. While property was damaged, no lives were lost on the last day of a holiday weekend when many people were outdoors camping or doing other recreational activities.
episodes.168151: A line of thunderstorms that developed over northern Iowa Monday evening, May 30th, moved northeast and re-intensified over west central Wisconsin late in the night, during the very early hours of May 31. This line produced wind damage with a few trees blown down or uprooted from near Eau Claire/Chippewa Falls, northeast toward Cornell.

episodes.168294: Abundant moisture, in combination with strong daytime heating, provided the fuel for robust thunderstorm development along a quasi-stationary front located across the southern Texas Panhandle late on the afternoon of the 31st. Strong instability and moderate wind shear allowed the storms which formed to quickly become severe and gain mid-level rotation. The rotating storms were efficient at generating hail, including very large hail at times. Several locations near Memphis (Hall County) and Tulia (Swisher County) reported hail as large 3 to 3.5 inches in diameter. The giant hail, bigger than baseballs, destroyed windshields on numerous vehicles on US Highway Highway 287 in Hall County. The intense and excessive rainfall flooded out a number of roadways across the southeast Texas Panhandle, including in and around Memphis. This event carried over into the early morning hours of June first.
episodes.168866: There was a large upper level trough over the western part of the country and a dryline across West Texas. An elevated temperature inversion was in place across the area with high instability above the inversion. Fairly high moisture east of the dryline and wind shear were also present. The higher terrain in and around the Davis Mountains and Big Bend areas allowed for air to rise and thunderstorms to develop. These storms resulted in large hail and severe wind gusts across Pecos and Brewster Counties.
episodes.169040: An extremely unstable airmass was in place across southern Kansas on May 31st as storms erupted along a stationary front from western Oklahoma into southern Kansas. Storms quickly became severe producing very large hail along with a couple brief tornadoes. In addition, they also produced very heavy rain that caused flash flooding along with subsequent river flooding.
episodes.169217: Thunderstorms moved through central and south central Kansas during the evening into the overnight hours. These storms produced quarter sized hail and 60 to 70 mph winds. Heavy rainfall associated with the storms led to flash flooding as well in central Kansas.
episodes.169273: Iowa was placed within the warm sector of a strong surface low pressure system, and the tight pressure gradient and deep mixing allowed for gusty south winds. A handful of station even gusted over 50 kts with some damage reported. Meanwhile, a dryline initiated convection across parts of northern Iowa in the late afternoon and evening. These storm primarily produced strong winds, though quarter sized hail was reported by one observer. Later that night, the cold front brought through another round of non-severe thunderstorms.
episodes.169359: A summer pattern was in place with a moist and unstable airmass in the afternoon.  As a result, few strong to severe storms affected the area with impacts to trees and powerlines across portions of Jefferson and Madison counties.
episodes.169365: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed in a moist and unstable airmass with one report of severe weather received.
episodes.169376: A summer pattern was in place with scattered showers and thunderstorms across the coastal waters.  A few gusts in excess of 34 knots were measured.
episodes.169663: Another 1 to 1.5 inches of rainfall on May 30 in northeast and east central South Dakota brought back minor flooding to upper portions of the Big Sioux River.
episodes.169676: Storms developed along a stationary boundary in northwestern Oklahoma into the Texas panhandle during the afternoon and evening of the 31st. Slow storm motions led to very heavy rainfall and flooding in some locations. Intense winds close to 80 mph, large hail, and a few tornadoes were also reported.
episodes.169716: A complex of storms developed along a cold front across the southeast Texas Panhandle. A leading supercell moved through southern Collingsworth County where it exhibited strong rotation as it moved through an area with sufficient low level winds shear. This supercell then developed 2 separate tornadoes, one northwest of Dodson, Texas and the second over southern portions of Dodson. Both tornadoes were rated EF-0 with max winds of 85 MPH with tree damage and some structures damaged along the tornadoes path.
episodes.169844: Supercells developed along a front and produced hail, strong winds and some flash flooding during the afternoon and evening of 5/30.
episodes.169845: There were a few thunderstorms that produced near quarter sized hail in two counties during the evening of 5/31.
episodes.170023: A strong area of low pressure across the Northern Plains lifted a warm front across the Northland on Memorial Day morning. Showers and storms moved through during the morning hours with the atmosphere recovering during the afternoon hours. A few of the storms were severe during the morning and produced small hail and tree damage. An arc of thunderstorms developed across southwestern Minnesota and adjacent areas of Nebraska, South Dakota and Iowa by the mid-afternoon hours and moved to the northeast and across the Northland for the late afternoon and evening hours. These storms were much stronger and contained very strong winds that produced widespread damage across the region. Additionally, there were a few embedded tornadoes with the storms with the strongest tornadoes producing EF-1 damage in the Deer River and Hinckley areas.
episodes.170024: A strong area of low pressure across the Northern Plains lifted a warm front across the Northland on Memorial Day morning. Showers and storms moved through during the morning hours with the atmosphere recovering during the afternoon hours An arc of thunderstorms developed across southwestern Minnesota and adjacent areas of Nebraska, South Dakota and Iowa by the mid-afternoon hours and moved to the northeast and across the Northland for the late afternoon and evening hours. As the storms moved into northwest Wisconsin, they quickly weekend and only produced sporadic wind damage as they raced to the northeast.
episodes.170125: An enhanced risk in the area resulted in some 1-inch hail reports and 58-65 mph winds.
episodes.170206: A line of fast moving storms moved across portions of northeast Iowa during the evening of May 30th. These storms produced wind gusts between 60 and 70 mph that blew down trees in Rudd (Floyd County). A spotter measured a 72 mph gust near Rockford (Floyd County).
episodes.170213: A line of fast moving storms moved across portions of southeast Minnesota during the evening of May 30th. A 67 mph gust occurred just east of Whalan (Fillmore County) and at the Rochester (Olmsted County) airport. Trees and power lines were down in Preston (Fillmore County).
episodes.170408: There was barely a break between the exit of the earlier morning severe convection, and development of the next round during the afternoon and early evening on May 30th across southwest Minnesota.  A series of impulses moved northeast during the day, with a leading strong wave moving out of Nebraska by early afternoon. Storms blossomed near a cold frontal boundary toward the James River Valley, despite the limited diurnal destabilization, due to steep mid-level lapse rates which brought MLCAPE up to 1500-2000J/kg in the warm sector. Strong mid-level winds led to long, linear hodographs. With a warm front also lingering north of Interstate 90, storms that interacted with enhanced low-level shear in the vicinity of various boundaries produced a few brief tornadoes, but strong deep-layer forcing eventually resulted in an evolution toward linear structures with mainly damaging wind.  Near the core of the upper level wave, a secondary band of thunderstorms developed across Nebraska during the late afternoon and raced northeastward through early evening, featuring mainly damaging wind gusts.
episodes.170475: A potent low-pressure system impacted the region during the afternoon and evening hours of May 30th. A larger scale Derecho tracked from far southeastern South Dakota, through much of western through northcentral Minnesota. Widespread damage was reported from damaging winds, and tornadoes. Hail up to 1.5 inches was reported as well.
episodes.170476: A potent low-pressure system impacted the region during the afternoon and evening hours of May 30th. Wind damage was reported in portions of southeastern North Dakota.

Damage sustained to a fast food restaurant in Hinckley, including broken windows, a damaged rooftop HVAC unit, and evidence of metal flashing damage, is believed to be the beginning of a tornado that then tracked across Interstate 35 in a north-northwest direction, crossing the railroad tracks near 7th St NE. The majority of the damage was trees uprooted with several snapped along the way. Aerial imagery provided by the Pine County Sheriff���s Department shows fairly weak but convergent tree fall between I-35 and near Highway 61 and Owl Drive between a distinct intensification where the treefall becomes much more extensive and a metal roof section was lifted off a local business. The tornado then tracked across Highway 61 and traversed north causing mainly tree damage with at least one home losing some roof shingles. The end of the tornado path is estimated due to the track moving into a much less wooded wetland area. NWS Duluth sincerely appreciates the drone imagery provided by the Pine County Sheriff���s Office to aid in the assessment of this storm damage. Peak winds were estimated to be 95 mph.
